question: Is the mid-latitude over-representation of hollow fields (panel d of net_fig1_v2) informative about the material or process?
finding_1_null_dependence: The residual profile depends on the completeness null. Size-marginalized null: 0.65/0.70/1.02/0.98/2.10/2.59/1.72/0.83 (0-80N by 10 deg). Fixed 1-km null: 1.38/1.27/1.34/0.84/1.22/1.19/0.67/0.32. At FIXED best resolution (<=40 m) field density per searched area is 42/56/73/48/68/76/47/29 per 1e6 km2 -> a ~1.5-1.8x mid-latitude (20-60) enhancement and a >60N deficit; in the 40-80 m class the equator is the DENSEST band (33 vs 12-21). Most of the 4x contrast in panel d is the completeness model, whose equatorial values depend on assumed hollow size.
finding_2_geology: Klima LRM by band 6.8/5.6/8.1/5.2/11.4/2.4/0.6/1.0 and crater-interior fraction 0.36-0.50 do not track the 50-70N excess (LRM is lowest there). The 40-70N excess is not zonal: 154 of 313 fields sit in 90-150E (obs/expected 5.2 and 4.6), a province NE of Caloris with several 80-120-hollow fields; sectors 30-60E and 180-210E are deficits (0.35, 0.49). Northern smooth plains explain the >70N deficit.
finding_3_illumination: Median frame incidence rises 51 -> 79 deg with latitude; fraction of frames >60 deg 0.40 -> 1.00. Relief-only (degraded) hollows are visible only at high incidence (stage_vs_incidence.json), so detectability of the degraded population rises with latitude in a way the completeness model (fitted on halo-bearing repeat detections, b_inc weak) does not capture. This biases toward a mid/high-latitude excess and against the equator.
finding_4_lifetime: Degraded-stage fraction after controlling incidence and resolution shows NO equatorial excess (-0.015, -0.033 at 0-20N); it is negative at 60-80N. Pixel-scale-controlled depth is 0.08 dex shallower at 0-20N and 0.18-0.32 dex shallower at 60-80N than mid-latitudes. The 'equatorial hollows die fast and are Stage 3' hypothesis predicts an excess of degraded stages and shallow depths at the equator; the first is absent, the second is weak. Truly dead hollows are invisible to the catalogue, so the hypothesis is not excluded, only unsupported by what is observable.
finding_5_thermal: Mercury's 3:2 resonance makes hot-pole longitudes (0, 180E) ~2.5x hotter at peak than warm-pole longitudes (90, 270E) at low latitude. Hollow fields at 0-15N are 1.31x over-represented at hot-pole longitudes and 0.67x at warm-pole (hot/warm 1.9; 1.86 with Caloris excluded); 15-30N: 1.67 (1.58). Hollows are MORE common where insolation is strongest, consistent with insolation driving formation/exposure (cf. equator-facing scarps), not with thermal exhaustion at the equator. At 45-60N the ratio inverts (0.43) because the 90-150E province sits at warm-pole longitudes.
interpretation: The latitude distribution is only weakly informative once imaging is controlled: a modest 20-60N enhancement that is mostly one longitude province, a >60N deficit (northern smooth plains), and a low-latitude preference for hot-pole longitudes. Of the PI's three candidates, geological control (province-scale distribution of hollow-forming material, and LRM only partly) fits best; differential lifetime is unsupported by stage and depth; a residual illumination bias in the catalogue is likely and unmodeled.
next_tests: Rebuild the completeness null with an incidence term fitted on relief-only detections, or restrict to frames with incidence 60-75 at all latitudes
Map the 90-150E, 40-70N province geologically (units, LRM, crater ages) - it hosts half the mid-latitude excess
Extend the hot/warm-pole test to the southern hemisphere with the corrected positions
Aspect statistics (Thomas 2014 n=31) on the full corrected catalogue: if hot-pole preference is insolation-driven, scarps should face the subsolar direction
